[{:db/id 17592186166816 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" "question-615e1fed-a4a8-59b3-8748-a44e86a3ce62" "question-e8cab3f8-2d4f-5187-b7bf-4e4ac59dbfe4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" :question/id #uuid "967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" :question/math-academy-id "q-96847" :question/problem "Given $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ compute $P(X=5),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\frac{{2}^{x}{e}^{-2}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{5}{e}^{-2}}{5!} \\  & ≈0.0361.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de" :answer-field/id #uuid "11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" "answer-92fa4d3d-3196-543c-b2e9-3de9e87a5486" "answer-4266e4f5-01a4-59c0-9d1a-6a59858398c5" "answer-8d665c00-37aa-5b15-bca3-222341cd0fb8" "answer-d62cc53f-5c2d-54bf-8c03-97c83dc95c5b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer/id #uuid "78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.0361" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92fa4d3d-3196-543c-b2e9-3de9e87a5486" :answer/id #uuid "92fa4d3d-3196-543c-b2e9-3de9e87a5486" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.0802" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4266e4f5-01a4-59c0-9d1a-6a59858398c5" :answer/id #uuid "4266e4f5-01a4-59c0-9d1a-6a59858398c5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.0842" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d665c00-37aa-5b15-bca3-222341cd0fb8" :answer/id #uuid "8d665c00-37aa-5b15-bca3-222341cd0fb8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1014" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d62cc53f-5c2d-54bf-8c03-97c83dc95c5b" :answer/id #uuid "d62cc53f-5c2d-54bf-8c03-97c83dc95c5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1115" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-615e1fed-a4a8-59b3-8748-a44e86a3ce62" :question/id #uuid "615e1fed-a4a8-59b3-8748-a44e86a3ce62" :question/math-academy-id "q-130050" :question/problem "Given $X∼\text{Po}(5),$ compute $P(X=3),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$-\frac{5}{3x}=\frac{5}{6}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{3x}{5}=\frac{6}{5}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{5} & =\frac{6}{5} \\ (-5)\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{-5}\right) & =(-5)\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ (\cancel{-5})\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{\cancel{-5}}\right) & =(\cancel{5})\cdot \frac{-6}{\cancel{5}} \\ 3x & =-6 \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{6}{3} \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2b3d2617-e9dc-5524-9ebf-d810c3ed7f04"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2b3d2617-e9dc-5524-9ebf-d810c3ed7f04" :answer-field/id #uuid $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{3x}{2}=\frac{9}{2}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ (-2)\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{-2}\right) & =(-2)\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\ \cancel{(-2)}\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{\cancel{-2}}\right) & =\cancel{2}\cdot \frac{-9}{\cancel{2}} \\ 3x & =-9 \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)(-9) \\ \cancel{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{9}{3} \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}

$$

"Solve the equation $\frac{2}{x+5}=\frac{1}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{2}=\frac{4}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
\frac{x+5}{2}=4
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \left(\frac{x+5}{2}\right) & =2\cdot 4 \\ \cancel{2}\cdot \left(\frac{x+5}{\cancel{2}}\right) & =8 \\ x+5 & =8 \\ x+5-5 & =8-5 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}

#uuid "af124b69-d0c1-5851-8687-aa12571f64c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-67424" :question/problem "Solve the equation  $\frac{1}{2x+1}=\frac{3}{5x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{1}=\frac{5x}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $3.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{6x+3}{3}=\frac{5x}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{6x+3}{3} & =3\cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\ 6x+3 & =5x \\ 6x+3-3 & =5x-3 \\ 6x & =5x-3 \\ 6x-5x & =5x-3-5x \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2033eef-36dd-539d-9289-20b6ea9c55f6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b2033eef-36dd-539d-9289-20b6ea9c55f6" :answer-field/id #uuid "e5e7057b-4215-507e-8d16-5466bad05ab6" :question/math-academy-id "q-67441" :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{5}{2x+1}=\frac{1}{x+1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{x+1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $5.$ The equation becomes

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{5x+5}{5}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5)\cdot \frac{2x+1}{5} & =(5)\cdot \frac{5x+5}{5} \\ 2x+1 & =5x+5 \\ 1-5 & =5x-2x \\ -4 & =3x \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-4) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-4) & =(\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) \\ -\frac{4}{3} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

{"source" ":org/Math-Academy" "forms" [{:db/id 17592186166816 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" "question-615e1fed-a4a8-59b3-8748-a44e86a3ce62" "question-e8cab3f8-2d4f-5187-b7bf-4e4ac59dbfe4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" :question/id #uuid "967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" :question/math-academy-id "q-96847" :question/problem "Given $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ compute $P(X=5),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\frac{{2}^{x}{e}^{-2}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{5}{e}^{-2}}{5!} \\  & ≈0.0361.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de" :answer-field/id #uuid "11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" "answer-92fa4d3d-3196-543c-b2e9-3de9e87a5486" "answer-4266e4f5-01a4-59c0-9d1a-6a59858398c5" "answer-8d665c00-37aa-5b15-bca3-222341cd0fb8" "answer-d62cc53f-5c2d-54bf-8c03-97c83dc95c5b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer/id #uuid "78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.0361" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92fa4d3d-3196-543c-b2e9-3de9e87a5486" :answer/id #uuid "92fa4d3d-3196-543c-b2e9-3de9e87a5486" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.0802" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4266e4f5-01a4-59c0-9d1a-6a59858398c5" :answer/id #uuid "4266e4f5-01a4-59c0-9d1a-6a59858398c5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.0842" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d665c00-37aa-5b15-bca3-222341cd0fb8" :answer/id #uuid "8d665c00-37aa-5b15-bca3-222341cd0fb8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1014" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d62cc53f-5c2d-54bf-8c03-97c83dc95c5b" :answer/id #uuid "d62cc53f-5c2d-54bf-8c03-97c83dc95c5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1115" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-615e1fed-a4a8-59b3-8748-a44e86a3ce62" :question/id #uuid "615e1fed-a4a8-59b3-8748-a44e86a3ce62" :question/math-academy-id "q-130050" :question/problem "Given $X∼\text{Po}(5),$ compute $P(X=3),$ rounded to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$-\frac{5}{3x}=\frac{5}{6}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{3x}{5}=\frac{6}{5}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{5} & =\frac{6}{5} \\ (-5)\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{-5}\right) & =(-5)\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ (\cancel{-5})\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{\cancel{-5}}\right) & =(\cancel{5})\cdot \frac{-6}{\cancel{5}} \\ 3x & =-6 \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{6}{3} \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2b3d2617-e9dc-5524-9ebf-d810c3ed7f04"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2b3d2617-e9dc-5524-9ebf-d810c3ed7f04" :answer-field/id #uuid "Solve the equation $\frac{2}{x+5}=\frac{1}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{2}=\frac{4}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
\frac{x+5}{2}=4
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication and the addition principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \left(\frac{x+5}{2}\right) & =2\cdot 4 \\ \cancel{2}\cdot \left(\frac{x+5}{\cancel{2}}\right) & =8 \\ x+5 & =8 \\ x+5-5 & =8-5 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{6}{1}=\frac{x-7}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
-6=x-7
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =x-7 \\ -6+7 & =x-7+7 \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

#uuid "af124b69-d0c1-5851-8687-aa12571f64c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-67424" :question/problem "Solve the equation  $\frac{1}{2x+1}=\frac{3}{5x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{1}=\frac{5x}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $3.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{6x+3}{3}=\frac{5x}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{6x+3}{3} & =3\cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\ 6x+3 & =5x \\ 6x+3-3 & =5x-3 \\ 6x & =5x-3 \\ 6x-5x & =5x-3-5x \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b2033eef-36dd-539d-9289-20b6ea9c55f6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b2033eef-36dd-539d-9289-20b6ea9c55f6" :answer-field/id #uuid "e5e7057b-4215-507e-8d16-5466bad05ab6" :question/math-academy-id "q-67441" :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{5}{2x+1}=\frac{1}{x+1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{x+1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $5.$ The equation becomes

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{5x+5}{5}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5)\cdot \frac{2x+1}{5} & =(5)\cdot \frac{5x+5}{5} \\ 2x+1 & =5x+5 \\ 1-5 & =5x-2x \\ -4 & =3x \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-4) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-4) & =(\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) \\ -\frac{4}{3} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{4}{3}.$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c08dc095-4a06-5102-a53c-3507e8db203b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ["question-967d2e95-57ac-5662-bd22-c0decd75429c" :question/worked-solution "If $X∼\text{Po}(\lambda ),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Po}(2),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)=\frac{{2}^{x}{e}^{-2}}{x!}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =f(5) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{5}{e}^{-2}}{5!} \\  & ≈0.0361.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-field-11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de" :answer-field/id #uuid "11838f10-dc22-5f3b-ba56-0d91440185de"] ["answer-78b3c30e-bbe9-50c9-a378-76cb62a0a57a" :answer/id #uuid We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3x}{5} & =\frac{6}{5} \\ (-5)\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{-5}\right) & =(-5)\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ (\cancel{-5})\cdot \left(\frac{3x}{\cancel{-5}}\right) & =(\cancel{5})\cdot \frac{-6}{\cancel{5}} \\ 3x & =-6 \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) & =-\frac{6}{3} \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-field-2b3d2617-e9dc-5524-9ebf-d810c3ed7f04" :answer-field/id #uuid "2b3d2617-e9dc-5524-9ebf-d810c3ed7f04"] ["answer-f71b448e-c54f-5b5b-8deb-0cb850d4f2ff" :answer/id #uuid We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{x+3}{7}
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition and the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{x+3}{7} \\ 7\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) & =7\cdot \left(\frac{x+3}{7}\right) \\ \frac{7}{2} & =\cancel{7}\cdot \left(\frac{x+3}{\cancel{7}}\right) \\ \frac{7}{2} & =x+3 \\ \frac{7}{2}-3 & =x+3-3 \\ \frac{1}{2} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

$$
-\frac{6}{1}=\frac{x-7}{1}
$$

$$
-6=x-7
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =x-7 \\ -6+7 & =x-7+7 \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Solve the equation  $\frac{1}{2x+1}=\frac{3}{5x}.$"] ["question-af124b69-d0c1-5851-8687-aa12571f64c4" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{1}=\frac{5x}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $3.$ The above equation becomes

$$
\frac{6x+3}{3}=\frac{5x}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{6x+3}{3} & =3\cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\ 6x+3 & =5x \\ 6x+3-3 & =5x-3 \\ 6x & =5x-3 \\ 6x-5x & =5x-3-5x \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-field-b2033eef-36dd-539d-9289-20b6ea9c55f6" :answer-field/id #uuid "b2033eef-36dd-539d-9289-20b6ea9c55f6"] ["answer-1eb090e7-b1fa-569e-a88c-88009df2442e" :answer/id #uuid :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{5}{2x+1}=\frac{1}{x+1}.$"] ["question-e5e7057b-4215-507e-8d16-5466bad05ab6" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{x+1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $5.$ The equation becomes

$$
\frac{2x+1}{5}=\frac{5x+5}{5}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5)\cdot \frac{2x+1}{5} & =(5)\cdot \frac{5x+5}{5} \\ 2x+1 & =5x+5 \\ 1-5 & =5x-2x \\ -4 & =3x \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-4) & =\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (3x) \\ \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot (-4) & =(\cancel{\frac{1}{3}})\cdot (\cancel{3}x) \\ -\frac{4}{3} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{4}{3}.$"] ["answer-field-c08dc095-4a06-5102-a53c-3507e8db203b" :answer-field/id #uuid "c08dc095-4a06-5102-a53c-3507e8db203b"] $$

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$

$$

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero, and

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{x-2} = \dfrac 3{5x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x-2}{1} = \dfrac{5x}{3}
$$

The above equation simplifies to 

$$
x-2 = \dfrac{5x}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot (x-2) & =3\cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\ 3x-6 & =5x \\ 3x-5x & =6 \\ -2x & =6 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048725} {:db/id 17592186060373 :question/id #uuid "04e7e1a5-bfd5-5b88-b6d7-211b2707b8d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-67328"} {:db/id 17592186060376 :question/id #uuid "09320d7a-d867-531b-9740-66504912149d" :question/math-academy-id "q-67332" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059708 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c2c24d70-3bde-5277-bc92-ae081065deee" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial and a Monomial in Denominators"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9afe93af-c815-5f2c-ac75-9a584d561ee5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186058879} {:answer/id #uuid "e4d50060-ed5a-55ba-98a5-e136d622f6bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7}{4}" :db/id 17592186058880} {:answer/id #uuid "e6d7edad-f24a-5a39-b3a9-bdf0e222d37a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{7}" :db/id 17592186058881} {:answer/id #uuid "3af8e372-8b94-5bca-966e-b13590d4c251" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{4}{7}" :db/id 17592186058882} {:answer/id #uuid "4335e387-f8cb-50d1-a3a5-f1a739c9876b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186058883}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3af8e372-8b94-5bca-966e-b13590d4c251" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{4}{7}" :db/id 17592186058882} :answer-field/id #uuid "084ec80c-c0ed-58a4-b621-614f03d00659" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186058878}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{2}{3x+2}=-\frac{4}{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot \left(-\frac{x}{4}\right) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503661 :question/id #uuid "1a235d31-7002-5190-8de9-b78ca920ac5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-67425" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059708 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c2c24d70-3bde-5277-bc92-ae081065deee" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial and a Monomial in Denominators"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "55a6fcca-aad9-5ad1-a121-fdaf665d5aad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186503145} {:answer/id #uuid "d92f70d4-3067-5353-97b7-e64c25a54de0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186503415} {:answer/id #uuid "dcb302e9-c203-5981-98a6-1abb4868178a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186503427} {:answer/id #uuid "e0db71b8-ad73-5cce-b817-b4e5c4f03d39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186503441} {:answer/id #uuid "ecb895ed-3b69-53d2-9ba7-f858762d5ad6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186503466}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "dcb302e9-c203-5981-98a6-1abb4868178a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186503427} :answer-field/id #uuid "fbaaab81-294e-5a37-9fb1-b73c2d58a5c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186503643}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Solve the equation $-\frac{3}{x}=\frac{9}{3x-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=\frac{1}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x}{3}=\frac{3x-1}{9}
$$

$$
-\frac{3x}{9}=\frac{3x-1}{9}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9)\cdot \frac{3x}{-9} & =(-9)\cdot \frac{3x-1}{9} \\ 3x & =(-1)\cdot (3x-1) \\ 3x & =1-3x \\ 3x+3x & =1-3x+3x \\ 6x & =1 \\ \left(\frac{1}{6}\right)\cdot 6x & =\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)\cdot 1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503729 :question/id #uuid "b01bcc83-5d54-554e-8eb4-318389e1d142" :question/math-academy-id "q-67422" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186059708 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c2c24d70-3bde-5277-bc92-ae081065deee" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Rational Equations with a Binomial and a Monomial in Denominators"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e09809f-1ac1-5163-95fe-56a6c3cca096" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186503015} {:answer/id #uuid "1702597c-5660-544c-a89c-cba9f00560d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186503028} {:answer/id #uuid "2f7989a1-6ce6-581c-a185-11e1a6852423" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186503069} {:answer/id #uuid "78dcdf47-9629-5ab8-a15d-6bafe37b89e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186503225} {:answer/id #uuid "94f3bb0d-e212-55c1-a64b-282f04cc5137" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186503274}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2f7989a1-6ce6-581c-a185-11e1a6852423" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186503069} :answer-field/id #uuid "e4d1887c-0c5d-5ac5-9c0f-77c952d10182" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186503629}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{6}{x+2}=\frac{3}{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

$$

$$

We conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186059709 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059522 :question/id #uuid "13f9fd01-802e-5331-b422-b9aa2cdda7ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-4236"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "387a794f-17ea-5ea9-86a1-656a495f62cb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048213}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060374 :question/id #uuid "8b4e7858-1264-5def-86e5-7598a8adf5a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-67329"} {:db/id 17592186060375 :question/id #uuid "aecc8831-87b9-53b2-877d-65c0b164800c" :question/math-academy-id "q-67331"} {:db/id 17592186234237 :question/id #uuid "aa75fc9d-104d-5e12-b331-4d8ff3973336" :question/math-academy-id "q-67439"} {:db/id 17592186503706 :question/id #uuid "7e3eaae0-125c-585a-90f2-bbc8b4da35cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-106354"} {:db/id 17592186540100 :question/id #uuid "dba16e2f-f755-5c6f-b25b-801d348b9282" :question/math-academy-id "q-67435"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Rational Equations with Binomials in Both Denominators"} {:db/id 17592186059522 :question/id #uuid "13f9fd01-802e-5331-b422-b9aa2cdda7ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-4236" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186059709 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "387a794f-17ea-5ea9-86a1-656a495f62cb" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Rational Equations with Binomials in Both Denominators"}] :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac 1{2x-1} = \dfrac{1}{x+1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=\dfrac 12$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero, and

- $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{2x-1} = \dfrac{1}{x+1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{2x-1}{1} = \dfrac{x+1}1
$$

$$

$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =x+1 \\ 2x-x & =1+1 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}

- $x=3$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-6$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x-3}{6}=\frac{x+6}{2}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $6.$ The equation becomes

$$
\frac{x-3}{6}=\frac{3x+18}{6}.
$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{1}{x+5}=\frac{3}{2x+12}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=-6$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{2x+12}{3}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $3.$ We get

$$
\frac{3x+15}{3}=\frac{2x+12}{3}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \left(\frac{3x+15}{3}\right) & =3\cdot \left(\frac{2x+12}{3}\right) \\ 3x+15 & =2x+12 \\ 3x-2x & =12-15 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot \left(\frac{x-2}{-4}\right) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot (5x) & =\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Po}(5)$, so the probability distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{5^x e^{-5}}{x!}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X < 3) &= P(X ∈ {0, 1, 2}) \\
&= P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2) \\
&= f(0) + f(1) + f(2) \\
&= \frac{5^{0}e^{-5}}{0!} + \frac{5^{1}e^{-5}}{1!} + \frac{5^{2}e^{-5}}{2!} \\
&\approx 0.1247
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167444 :question/id #uuid "f573dedd-303f-5578-8aa1-2cdbc2e1a780" :question/math-academy-id "q-95994"} {:db/id 17592186167486 :question/id #uuid "69657179-8331-58e5-80f1-2a059b2270af" :question/math-academy-id "q-96880"} {:db/id 17592186166818 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166656 :question/id #uuid "c89b3081-38d7-5430-b912-82f84ef532ec" :question/math-academy-id "e-8467"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "21835800-1a05-56c1-a5ee-b8c2e1df2273" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167445 :question/id #uuid "b0aaec70-a36a-51f3-8298-8f57d534ba8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95995"} {:db/id 17592186167487 :question/id #uuid "d1087864-b8f1-5bc8-82f1-6691b2656da9" :question/math-academy-id "q-96892"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Over a Bounded Interval: Lower Bound is Not Zero"} {:db/id 17592186166656 :question/id #uuid "c89b3081-38d7-5430-b912-82f84ef532ec" :question/math-academy-id "e-8467" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166818 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "21835800-1a05-56c1-a5ee-b8c2e1df2273" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Over a Bounded Interval: Lower Bound is Not Zero"}] :question/problem "Given $X \sim \textrm{Po}(3)$, compute $P(2 < X < 5)$, rounded to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda)$, then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Po}(3)$, so the probability distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(2 < X < 5) &= P(X ∈ {3, 4}) \\
&= P(X = 3) + P(X = 4) \\
&= f(3) + f(4) \\
&= \frac{3^{3}e^{-3}}{3!} + \frac{3^{4}e^{-3}}{4!} \\
&\approx 0.3921
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167445 :question/id #uuid "b0aaec70-a36a-51f3-8298-8f57d534ba8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95995"} {:db/id 17592186167487 :question/id #uuid "d1087864-b8f1-5bc8-82f1-6691b2656da9" :question/math-academy-id "q-96892"} {:db/id 17592186166819 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166657 :question/id #uuid "d1e693a2-073f-5f8c-98fd-3b89496521d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8468"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6219a2a-8c28-57c1-a4ad-0ede62529376" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049642}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167446 :question/id #uuid "12fdf789-327a-5f92-8961-b43089eabcb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-95996"} {:db/id 17592186167488 :question/id #uuid "c793a448-fb8a-57b2-8e18-9e4de27af1b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-96901"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Over an Unbounded Interval Using the Complement"} {:db/id 17592186166657 :question/id #uuid "d1e693a2-073f-5f8c-98fd-3b89496521d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8468" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166819 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6219a2a-8c28-57c1-a4ad-0ede62529376" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Probability Over an Unbounded Interval Using the Complement"}] :question/problem "Given $X \sim \textrm{Po}(3)$, compute $P(X > 2)$, rounded to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda)$, then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}
$$

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Po}(3)$, so the probability distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X > 2$. However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X > 2) &= 1 - P(X \le 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X \le 2) &= P(X ∈ {0, 1, 2}) \\
&= P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2) \\
&= f(0) + f(1) + f(2) \\
&= \frac{3^{0}e^{-3}}{0!} + \frac{3^{1}e^{-3}}{1!} + \frac{3^{2}e^{-3}}{2!} \\
&\approx 0.4232
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X > 2) &= 1 - P(X \le 2) \\
&\approx 1 - 0.4232 \\
&= 0.5768
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049642} {:db/id 17592186167446 :question/id #uuid "12fdf789-327a-5f92-8961-b43089eabcb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-95996"} {:db/id 17592186167488 :question/id #uuid "c793a448-fb8a-57b2-8e18-9e4de27af1b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-96901"} {:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186048934} {:db/id 17592186048956} {:db/id 17592186049899} {:db/id 17592186050688 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429350 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. value of the function $f(x,y) = 3x^2 - y^2$ given that $3x^2 + 2y^2\leq 16.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨6x,-2y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=\left(0,  0 \right).$ This point belongs to our region.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= 3x^2 + 2y^2  = 16.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨6x,-2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨6x,4y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}6x &=6\lambda x \\ -2y &=4\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(2\lambda +1) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  =16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,y=\pm 2\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0, \pm 2\sqrt 2 \right).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  =16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,x=\pm \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(\pm \dfrac{4\sqrt 3}{3}, 0 \right).$

- Note that assuming $\lambda = 1$ from the first equation leads to $y=0,$ which we already have a solution for, and $\lambda = -\dfrac12$ from the second equation leads to $x=0,$ which we also have a solution for. So, we have found all the candidates on the boundary.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
\left( 0,0 \right), \qquad  \left( 0, \pm 2\sqrt 2 \right), \qquad \left(\pm \dfrac{4\sqrt 3}{3}, 0\right).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $\left( 0,0 \right)$ | $\left( 0, \pm 2\sqrt 2 \right)$ | $\left( \pm \dfrac{4\sqrt 3}{3}, 0 \right)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $-8$ | $16$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $\left(0, \pm 2\sqrt 2  \right),$ and its minimum value is $-8.$"} {:db/id 17592186048162} {:db/id 17592186199017 :question/id #uuid "ab0253d0-1db9-532d-bb4a-604c88a16da0" :question/math-academy-id "q-98103" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "839287e3-b143-5415-99de-08e22d1fe7ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "42" :db/id 17592186197973} {:answer/id #uuid "9ac8fd50-dcb6-5b86-b402-c970434163b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186197974} {:answer/id #uuid "fca362ab-06c7-5e0f-a0ea-d44fa5a42449" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36" :db/id 17592186197975} {:answer/id #uuid "401f21c4-4ada-5f5e-b68f-b4edd51e55ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186197976} {:answer/id #uuid "4d850692-8440-57f8-a931-14cb51d6f903" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186197977}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186197973} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b076631-de18-587b-978a-08fc530f03da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186197972}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x-4y$ given that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 18.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x-4,2y-4⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(2,2).$ This point belongs to our region.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=18.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=18
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x-4,2y-4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =1$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 1,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-4 &=2\lambda x \\ 2y-4 &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{2}{1-\lambda } \\ y &=\frac{2}{1-\lambda }\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ in the condition $g(x,y)=18,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =18 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =18 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =18 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(3,3),\,(-3,-3),\,(2,2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(3,3)$ | $(-3,-3)$ | $(2,2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-6$ | $42$ | $-8$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(-3,-3),$ and its maximum value is $42.$"} {:db/id 17592186199022 :question/id #uuid "73adc7f1-2e5c-592b-b8c9-bd080977f54f" :question/math-academy-id "q-99256" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "940363d2-e432-556a-b0c0-2c42895c1117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-40" :db/id 17592186198003} {:answer/id #uuid "20e54280-ff88-5af2-8610-6ef05e375392" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24" :db/id 17592186198004} {:answer/id #uuid "2740310c-d926-5b3d-916c-6755f45ae1b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-32" :db/id 17592186198005} {:answer/id #uuid "5bdb73f9-d522-5716-a40d-01eb373017ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-48" :db/id 17592186198006} {:answer/id #uuid "70c9a7e7-b1ad-5149-9703-aa84c63a4445" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186198007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186198006} :answer-field/id #uuid "dd5a22f3-e62c-5edf-b899-6619cb4a4071" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186198002}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}$ given that $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16.$ 

*Hint: The critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<16$ is $(0,0).$*" :question/worked-solution "We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨8x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=8\lambda x \\ -6y &=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda ) &=0 \\ y(3+\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,y=\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 4).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,x=\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 4),\,(\pm 2,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm 4)$ | $(\pm 2,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |

*Hint: The critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region ${x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}<25$ is $(0,0).$*" :question/worked-solution "We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}=25.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=25
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-16y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,10y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x &=2\lambda x \\ -16y &=10\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-\lambda ) &=0 \\ -2y(8+5\lambda ) &=0\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,x=\pm 5,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 5,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),\,(5,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm \sqrt{5})$ | $(\pm 5,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-40$ | $25$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),$ and its minimum value is $-40.$"} {:db/id 17592186281544 :question/id #uuid "6c8aaf19-7032-5c17-8488-1228e55d6f6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162782"} {:db/id 17592186281550 :question/id #uuid "a9f72078-f37a-504f-b398-fa5acaea8b10" :question/math-academy-id "q-162799"} {:db/id 17592186281583 :question/id #uuid "78ee316a-eb04-5e68-af98-0ccef9f21d29" :question/math-academy-id "q-163055"} {:db/id 17592186362348 :question/id #uuid "37949110-2c01-56b7-86c7-c788694289e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-99255" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9e208ac1-85a1-5e96-b7fa-52323bca0603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186361546} {:answer/id #uuid "a36edd82-90fe-5174-9433-626f33ab66c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186361567} {:answer/id #uuid "bfe3af3e-8a8f-5c90-9dc6-fba808b09e58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "40" :db/id 17592186361694} {:answer/id #uuid "c0a5aea1-7458-5a36-bfcd-ed941a842039" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186361700} {:answer/id #uuid "ca55e0f9-7162-5f22-b015-8e0165d10253" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186361751}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361694} :answer-field/id #uuid "6a1f27a1-0eda-517d-a4eb-016e3810f8d3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362073}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}+10{y}^{2}$ on the region ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$

$$

We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(0,0).$ This point belongs to our region.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+y=2.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=2
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives us the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x &=2\lambda x \\ -4y &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1-\lambda ) &=0 \\ y &=-\frac{\lambda }{4}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=2$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =1$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation gives $y=-\frac{1}{4},$ and the constraint condition $g(x,y)=2$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{4} & =2\,⇒\,x=\pm \frac{3}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm \frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{4}).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,0),\,(0,2),\,(\pm \frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{4}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(\pm \frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{4})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $-8$ | $\frac{17}{8}$ |

:question/math-academy-id "e-8691" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "849449fb-bb08-54a3-b8ea-9f33ddd7a3e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the maximum value of the sum of cosines of the angle measures of a triangle, given that all three angles are acute." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the measures of the angles. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = \cos{x}+\cos{y}+\cos{z},
$$

subject to the constraint

$$
x+y+z=\pi.
$$

Since the angles are acute, we also have the constraints $0 \lt x,y,z \lt \dfrac\pi 2.$ 

Let $g(x,y,z) = x+y+z.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y,z), \qquad g(x,y,z) = \pi
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,-\operatorname{sin}⁡z⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡y &=\lambda \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡z &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sine function is one-to-one on the interval $\left( 0, \dfrac \pi 2\right),$ we can conclude that $x = y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y =x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =\pi  \\ x+x+x & =\pi  \\ 3x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

It's easy to show that this point is indeed the maximum and not the minimum. To do that, we can compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{12}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{12}\right) \\  & ≈1.47 \\  & <f(\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198945 :question/id #uuid "5440dc48-4c46-5737-826b-cf98fbacdffa" :question/math-academy-id "q-37701"} {:db/id 17592186199018 :question/id #uuid "c427251e-04fb-5644-a763-9c09169a9227" :question/math-academy-id "q-98104" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "294a6497-3763-569f-bdf9-42356cd00564" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "54{\text{ cm}}^{3}" :db/id 17592186361019} {:answer/id #uuid "52b8263c-0e8f-52be-ba17-ae87e84b31f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32{\text{ cm}}^{3}" :db/id 17592186361202} {:answer/id #uuid "52e615b0-5300-5122-b210-2d048d12e825" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48{\text{ cm}}^{3}" :db/id 17592186361204} {:answer/id #uuid "96f252cb-20d0-588c-88d0-dd5df5d6f960" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24{\text{ cm}}^{3}" :db/id 17592186361510} {:answer/id #uuid "ed3d1ba2-d9d5-5815-a75e-960a8bfa5fbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36{\text{ cm}}^{3}" :db/id 17592186361890}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361202} :answer-field/id #uuid "62a25a4a-3331-5eca-802d-4fffe8f3048b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362066}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A rectangular box without a lid has a surface area of $48{\text{ cm}}^{2}.$ Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum possible volume of the box." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,y$, and $z$ be the box's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
2xz+2yz+xy=48.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=48
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}yz &=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz &=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy &=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}xyz &=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz &=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz &=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $xyz=0,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z\ne 0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz+2yz+xy & =48 \\ 4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =48 \\ 12{z}^{2} & =48 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(4,4,2),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(4,4,2)=4\cdot 4\cdot 2=32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,5.5) & =2\cdot 2\cdot 5.5 \\  & =22 \\  & <f(4,4,2).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281547 :question/id #uuid "b8c68071-089c-5bff-bc03-ba61a8eab03b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162788" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18f121e3-ccfa-57b8-b6ef-a2e2cd0f3b57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186278810} {:answer/id #uuid "65b8a4fe-1d29-5ee2-ad9f-6c0583668e1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186279516} {:answer/id #uuid "76c3a733-f198-5a7c-a7fb-0c39f1adc2a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186279650} {:answer/id #uuid "8bf6ea47-eaeb-5270-89ec-aea8d1830cbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186279837} {:answer/id #uuid "944923f9-e97d-5493-8850-5c83f2a0ed3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "29" :db/id 17592186279911}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279516} :answer-field/id #uuid "797a794d-3c44-5cfd-9959-01ae83cb5934" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281055}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the minimum possible sum of three positive numbers whose product is $27.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=\lambda yz \\ 1 &=\lambda xz \\ 1 &=\lambda xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362342 :question/id #uuid "1ec51af1-dbfa-5fa9-8f74-3c330eb163be" :question/math-academy-id "q-99163" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1609399a-f596-5865-ab9c-6aadc92d23db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "54\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186360926} {:answer/id #uuid "3a4ae6f5-4806-5c92-95fb-a3ec3dd390a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "42\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361102} {:answer/id #uuid "838bc3f9-5547-5aae-9ce5-c937af91a9a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "60\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361421} {:answer/id #uuid "83aec126-3e7b-519c-90b5-432b36990afa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "72\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361422} {:answer/id #uuid "8c4af1fe-8cbf-5c53-aeb4-2b02ab93e510" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48\,\text{in}" :db/id 17592186361456}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361421} :answer-field/id #uuid "e828baa6-f3ec-5068-b0c9-1c1c3f9d8a66" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362188}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A rectangular parallelepiped has a volume of $125\,{\text{in}}^{3}.$ Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the minimum sum of the lengths of its edges." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the rectangular parallelepiped's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=4x+4y+4z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=125.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=125
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨4,4,4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4 &=\lambda yz \\ 4 &=\lambda xz \\ 4 &=\lambda xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x &=\lambda xyz \\ 4y &=\lambda xyz \\ 4z &=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =125 \\ x(x)(x) & =125 \\ {x}^{3} & =125 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(5,5,5),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(5,5,5)=4(5)+4(5)+4(5)=60\,\text{in}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(25,5,1) & =4(25)+4(5)+4(1) \\  & =121 \\  & >f(5,5,5).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364648 :question/id #uuid "9021d181-6a6e-589c-8096-c7ad92921266" :question/math-academy-id "q-99230" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f027768c-f196-5e3f-adf4-7554b2177b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "243\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364650} {:answer/id #uuid "f96459e6-4979-5896-b4e6-40cb50e3fdd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "162\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364651} {:answer/id #uuid "5fe9f1a7-0904-5a92-b9f4-1e7ca2a2d4bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "128\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364652} {:answer/id #uuid "dc20d337-eb61-592e-aeed-865846e45bfb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "369\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364653} {:answer/id #uuid "42cfec62-7180-5eb9-8dbb-e33d7fe7ecf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364654} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ae58a56-6faf-52c9-9561-c87d35603ea0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364649}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A rectangular metal tank without a lid should hold $256\,{\text{ft}}^{3}$ of liquid. Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the tank's minimum possible surface area." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the tank's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=256.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=256
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨y+2z,x+2z,2x+2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=\lambda yz \\ x+2z &=\lambda xz \\ 2x+2y &=\lambda xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x(y+2z) &=\lambda xyz \\ y(x+2z) &=\lambda xyz \\ z(2x+2y) &=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(y+2z) & =y(x+2z) \\ xy+2xz & =xy+2yz \\ 2xz & =2yz \\ 2z(x-y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =256 \\ (2z)(2z)z & =256 \\ 4{z}^{3} & =256 \\ {z}^{3} & =64 \\ z & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(8,8,4),$ and the minimum value is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(8,8,4)=8(8)+2(8)(4)+2(8)(4)=192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(16,16,1) & =(16)(16)+2(16)(1)+2(16)(1) \\  & =320 \\  & >f(8,8,4).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186395878 :question/id #uuid "b8d6d6ad-6f2f-560c-8794-1cc77ef79232" :question/math-academy-id "q-37959"} {:db/id 17592186399343 :question/id #uuid "8e5f2d5d-b1b9-503b-9dbd-36de49acff81" :question/math-academy-id "q-99204" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08059ff9-d83f-540a-a482-2a8f806a18c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "105\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186399345} {:answer/id #uuid "40d83586-f330-5ddd-a884-c230dd198024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "125" :db/id 17592186399346} {:answer/id #uuid "591f3fa0-6797-5340-8094-49d07c9c3d89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "216" :db/id 17592186399347} {:answer/id #uuid "44d35100-e5d6-5e35-ac5b-f307d1753f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "256" :db/id 17592186399348} {:answer/id #uuid "1396c469-16f9-566a-aa93-62900910c424" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186399349}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186399347} :answer-field/id #uuid "25347463-2d58-522d-8979-b8544d1335f3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186399344}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum product of three positive numbers given that the sum of their squares is $108.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=108.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}yz &=2\lambda x \\ xz &=2\lambda y \\ xy &=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}xyz &=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz &=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz &=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =108 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(6,6,6),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,2,2) & =10\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =40 \\  & <f(6,6,6).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186446809 :question/id #uuid "1eb20554-7ec2-5620-86b4-093c81339236" :question/math-academy-id "q-99235"} {:db/id 17592186446810 :question/id #uuid "fb947756-3471-59c8-b3c4-9b21a1a91557" :question/math-academy-id "e-12457" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198405 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9bbc1e6a-c728-5c5a-84f8-06a92c30a023" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points"}] :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + y$ given that $2x^2 + 3y^2 \leq 1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= 2x^2 + 3y^2  = 1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \lambda \nabla g(x,y), \qquad g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,6y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x &=4\lambda x \\ 1 &=6\lambda y\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda ) &=0 \\ \lambda y &=\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  = 1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)^{2}+3{y}^{2}=1\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \right).$

- Assuming $\lambda = \dfrac12$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system gives 

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}y = \dfrac{1}{6} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad y = \dfrac1{3}.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)  =1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+3{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}=1\,⇒\,x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
\left(0,\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \right), \qquad  \left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right).
$$

 

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $\left(0, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$ | $\left(0, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$ | $\left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ | $-\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$ | $\dfrac{2}{3}$ |

 

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $\left(\pm \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac13 \right),$ and its maximum value is $\dfrac23.$"} {:db/id 17592186049390} {:db/id 17592186198946 :question/id
